info.title: DataSportsAPI
info.summary: Real-time sports data over REST for 25 sports — scores, schedules, lineups, match statistics, tables, and team, player and league profiles.
info.description:
One consistent JSON contract for 25 sports: fixtures and live scores, lineups and statistics, standings, plus teams, players and leagues, delivered in real time over REST, WebSocket and webhooks, with an MCP server for AI assistants.

Successful responses use a `{ data, meta? }` envelope; failures return `{ error: { code, message } }` under a matching HTTP status. All ids are DataSportsAPI ids. Each component schema documents its fields, units and enum values, as does the data model (https://datasportsapi.com/markdown/reference.md). The WebSocket stream, webhooks and widgets are documented at https://datasportsapi.com/docs/.

Availability: live. The Free plan allows 100 requests a day.

tags.name: catalog
tags.description: Sports & coverage. The starting point: which sports the API covers, which endpoint family serves each of them, how many of its matches are being played right now, and how much data sits behind it — leagues, teams, players, fixtures and how far back the seasons go.

tags.name: livescores
tags.description: Live scores. Fixtures that are in play right now. If you are building a live feature, the WebSocket is the better fit: it delivers the same objects and then pushes deltas.

tags.name: fixtures
tags.description: Fixtures. Look up fixtures by date, or fetch one match together with its detail sub-resources.

tags.name: teams
tags.description: Teams. A team is whoever takes part: a club, a national side, a tennis player, a fighter, a driver or a constructor. Profiles, fixtures, squads, transfers, season numbers, trophies and rankings live here.

tags.name: players
tags.description: Players. The people in a squad: profile, transfer history, the seasons they have numbers for, career tables, match ratings and heatmaps.

tags.name: leagues
tags.description: Leagues. A competition and everything inside one of its seasons: the table, rounds and fixtures, leaderboards, knockout brackets, team of the week and the season awards.

tags.name: discovery
tags.description: Rankings & directories. Starting points for finding ids: world rankings, plus the full set of a sport’s leagues by country or by category.

tags.name: races
tags.description: Races & series. Motorsport and cycling, the sports /v2/sports marks with kind races, are organised in three levels. The smallest is the session: one timed part, which can be practice, qualifying, a sprint, the race itself or a stage of a cycling race. Sessions make up a race, which is a whole Grand Prix weekend or one cycling race, and races make up a series, the counterpart of a league elsewhere (Formula 1, MotoGP; in cycling, the complete men’s or women’s calendar). Live changes are pushed on the race:{id} WebSocket channel (Business plan and up); over REST the same three things, the race, its list of sessions and the results of one session, each have an endpoint of their own. Two conventions hold throughout: times are in milliseconds and distances in metres, and a driver, a rider or a team is a TeamRef, so /v2/teams/{id} returns its profile.

tags.name: people
tags.description: Managers & referees. Fixture.referee carries referee ids; TeamDetail.manager and Fixture.homeManager / awayManager carry manager ids (each team’s current manager; the managers of a given match are on /v2/fixtures/{id}/managers). Both kinds can also be found through /v2/search. Football player agencies are here as well (since 2026-11-23): /v2/search with type=agency finds them, and /v2/agencies/{id} with its four lists shows whom each one represents, their contracts, their moves and their season.

tags.name: venues
tags.description: Venues. Venue ids appear on Fixture.venue and TeamDetail.venue, and /v2/search finds venues when you pass type=venue.

tags.name: search
tags.description: Search. One query across teams, players, leagues, managers, referees, series, races, fixtures and venues. The quickest way to the ids every other endpoint asks for.

tags.name: odds
tags.description: Odds. Odds are kept apart from match data. Fixtures, lists and stream deltas contain no betting fields, so nothing odds-related reaches your users unless you call the endpoints in this group or subscribe to the odds:{id} channel, the only two places where prices exist. The prices are those of a single bookmaker, before kick-off and in play, and reach us through our data source with no bookmaker named; they have been available since 2026-11-04. The endpoints are part of the Pro, Business and Enterprise plans, the live channel of Business and Enterprise. Before you show them, check the rules on displaying betting odds that apply where your users are, because they differ from place to place. The prices themselves come from a third party and are information only: not an offer to bet, and not betting advice. Adults only (18+); gamble responsibly.

tags.name: tracking
tags.description: Tracking. Enterprise only. These endpoints are the REST side of the tracking data, and the tracking:{id} WebSocket channel sends the same data as live frames. Two rules hold for all of it. Positions follow the coordinate frame named in TrackingSummary.coordinates, and that frame differs by sport. Darts has no coordinates at all; each dart is placed by the bed it landed in. Tennis uses millimetres, with the centre of the net as the origin. Football, basketball and ice hockey use a 0–100 grid on which the home side attacks towards x = 100 for the whole match. Baseball has none either: its entries say where the runners stand, not where anyone is. A player named in tracking data is a name from the match squad, without an id. What a match holds depends on its sport. Football: a ball track and events during play (the flow of play, meaning attack, dangerous attack, ball safe and change of possession, and within seconds also goals, shots, cards, substitutions and set pieces), followed after the match by the events with positions and passes. Tennis: the positions of the ball and the players as the match is played, with every serve and point. Basketball and ice hockey: a match timeline with the location of each shot, live since 2026-11-13; basketball has post-match events as well. Darts: a live timeline in which each dart and each visit is an entry (since 2026-11-13). Since 2026-11-24 table tennis and American football have live timelines too: every point in table tennis, which has no coordinates, and every play in American football, placed on a single axis of yards from the home goal line (field). Baseball joined on 2026-11-27 with a pitch-by-pitch timeline. Live positions of the players are not part of the API: only the live match tracker widget draws them. Tracking has been available since 2026-11-12, for matches from 2026-11-07 on.

tags.name: exports
tags.description: Season exports. This group turns one league season into downloadable files. The work happens in the background: the create call returns at once, the status call tells you when the build is done, and the finished export carries a download link for each file. The files hold the same data the season’s own endpoints return. An account may start 20 exports per UTC day, and every export is kept for 7 days. The group belongs to the Business and Enterprise plans and respects the plan’s history window: a season that had already ended when the window begins answers 403 history_not_in_plan. The window is 90 days on Business; Enterprise has no limit.

tags.name: websocket
tags.description: WebSocket. A push stream for Business and Enterprise accounts: once you subscribe to a channel, each change of score or status arrives as a delta, with no polling. Your API key stays out of the WebSocket URL. A REST call issues a ticket that works once, and the connection is opened with that. One channel, tracking:{id}, is reserved for Enterprise. A connection can hold up to 50 channel subscriptions, and the plan sets how many connections an account may keep open at once: 2 on Business and 5 on Enterprise.

get.description:
Lists all supported sports, each with the number of matches live right now. Matches the source has left open — 45 min without any change, with a kick-off further back than a match in that sport could run — do not count towards it. kind tells you which endpoint family serves the sport: fixtures, for sports served by the Fixtures, Teams and Leagues endpoints; races, for motorsport and cycling, which the Race sports endpoints cover (their fixture lists stay empty).

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
Coverage figures for the whole API in one call, open to every plan: entity totals, each sport’s league directory and how far back its headline competitions reach. The totals object counts how many teams, players, fixtures, leagues, seasons, venues, managers and referees have a DataSportsAPI id; each one can be fetched by that id, and the numbers never go down. The bySport list describes every sport’s directory — its categories (countries, tours, regions or games) with the leagues they hold, or the series for motorsport and cycling — together with up to ten headline competitions, each with its number of seasons and its first season; historyFrom is the earliest of those. The history object condenses the depth of all headline competitions into a median span in years and the oldest season. Old seasons are thinner than recent ones: results and tables usually go back further than lineups and statistics. updatedAt says when the figures were computed — totals every hour, directories once a day. A sport may be absent for a while after a restart, until its directory has been read again, and until the very first count is ready the endpoint answers 503 with Retry-After.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
Returns every live fixture across all sports, or one sport’s in-play board when ?sport= is set; each match reflects the live index, so its state is identical to the unfiltered call and to the WebSocket. Stale entries — no change for 45 min, and a start further back than a match in that sport can run — are dropped both here and on the WebSocket. Add ?finished=N (since 2026-11-25) to also get the matches that ended in the last N minutes.

**Note:** With finished=N (1–30), fixtures that ended within that many minutes (finished, canceled or abandoned) follow the live ones, most recent first, carrying their final status and score; meta then repeats finished and adds finishedCount. Leave it out and the list is the same as before. A fixture drops off the live list as soon as it ends, so when you poll this endpoint every few minutes, pass a finished value no shorter than your polling interval and no final result slips past.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

parameters.name: sport
parameters.description: sport slug as listed by /v2/sports, for example football

parameters.name: finished
parameters.description: minutes, 1 to 30: also return the fixtures that ended within that window, after the live ones; left out, only matches in play

meta.description: count, and sport if a filter was applied; finished and finishedCount when ?finished= is set

get.description:
Recent moments from the livescores channel, newest first, reaching back 7 days: score changes of any kind (goals, baskets, sets and runs, including corrections that lowered a score), red cards, kick-offs, period starts, breaks and final whistles. Every moment carries the score and status as they stood just after it, plus the ids and names of both sides, which is enough to fill a ticker before the WebSocket has delivered anything, or to show a client what happened while it was away for longer than replay covers. Each moment has exactly one kind, the first that fits in the order score, redCard, finished, break, kickoff, period. Available since 2026-11-16.

**Note:** Nothing older than 7 days is kept. The moments are recorded from the same changes the livescores channel publishes, as we publish them, and at is that publication time. To combine them with live deltas, match on fixtureId + kind + score.

**Plans:** Business and up; other plans receive 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

parameters.name: sport
parameters.description: sport slug; only that sport’s moments (all sports when left out)

parameters.name: since
parameters.description: ISO 8601 instant; only moments after it, for example the newest at you already hold

parameters.name: before
parameters.description: ISO 8601 instant; only moments before it, which pages backwards (send the oldest at you received)

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description: number of moments, 1–100 (30 when left out)

meta.description: count, sport (null when not filtered), limit

get.description:
Fixtures starting on one UTC date, for a single league, one category (country, region or tour, all its leagues at once), one country in a sport, a whole sport paged ten leagues at a time by league rank, or, with no sport, league or category at all, all sports at once (since 2026-11-24), sport after sport in a set order and each sport's leagues in the order of its own day list, ten leagues per page counted across sports, paged by cursor.

**Note:** Need a single country’s schedule, amateur and youth competitions included? Pass category= (take the id from that day’s /v2/fixtures/counts?sport= or from /v2/categories), or combine sport= with country=; either returns everything in one request rather than paging through the sport. To read a whole sport, or every sport, follow meta.nextCursor: send it back as cursor= until it comes back null. The cursor remembers which leagues you already have, so a league the source adds or moves between two reads can neither repeat a fixture nor drop one, as page offsets could; every page but the last holds 10 leagues that have fixtures that day, and added up, the pages agree with what /v2/fixtures/counts reports for the same sport and day. A busy day of every sport runs to a few hundred pages; /v2/fixtures/summary walks the same day in short rows, 50 leagues a page. Pass tz to read a local day instead of the UTC one. A Test or any other multi-day cricket match is listed on every day it is played, once per day (since 2026-11-24), from its start up to the day in its endTime; since 2026-11-26 a match the source has closed no longer turns up in the following day's list. A match the source forgot to close shows here with its in-play status and stale: true; /v2/livescores and the WebSocket drop it. The set of fixtures for a date is cached — for minutes on today and future dates, for hours on past dates, and permanently once every fixture has finished — whereas the status, score and clock of a live fixture are accurate to the second (see Update times). If you need a live feed, /v2/livescores or the WebSocket is the better fit.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

parameters.name: date
parameters.description: UTC date as YYYY-MM-DD (a local day with tz), from 1990-01-01 to one year in the future. A multi-day cricket match appears on each day it is played (since 2026-11-24)

parameters.name: sport
parameters.description: sport slug; leave sport, league and category all out to get every sport’s day, read by cursor (since 2026-11-24)

parameters.name: league
parameters.description: league id — returns only that league’s fixtures for the date, on a single page (page has to be 0)

parameters.name: category
parameters.description: category id, as listed by /v2/categories or /v2/fixtures/counts — all leagues of that country, region or tour for the date, sorted by start time, on a single page (page has to be 0). Available since 2026-11-04

parameters.name: country
parameters.description: two-letter Country.code (EN, ES, US …; case-insensitive), used together with sport — returns the date’s fixtures from that country’s categories in the sport, on a single page. Available since 2026-11-04

parameters.name: page
parameters.description: only when sport is the sole filter: page index 0–99 (defaults to 0), each page covering 10 leagues. A league with no fixture that day can leave a page short or even empty; cursor does not

parameters.name: cursor
parameters.description: the meta.nextCursor of the previous page, used instead of page with sport alone or with no filter at all. A cursor works for one hour and only with the sport and date it came from. Available since 2026-11-23

parameters.name: tz
parameters.description: reads date as a day in your own time: give an IANA zone name (Europe/London, America/New_York), which tracks summer time, so the day the clocks change is 23 or 25 hours long, or a plain offset from -12:00 to +14:00 (+03:00, -05:00, +3, +0530; send + encoded as %2B, since a bare + arrives as a space). You get the fixtures that begin inside that local day, with start times kept in UTC, and meta reports tz plus utcFrom and utcTo, where the day begins and ends in UTC. Leave tz out and the day is a UTC one. Available since 2026-11-24

meta.description: date, page, count, hasNextPage; the league filter adds league (and sport when passed), with page fixed at 0 and hasNextPage false; the category filter adds category (and sport when passed), single page; the country filter adds sport, country, categoryIds (the categories that were queried), complete; sport on its own, or no filter at all, adds sport (null for every sport), leagueCount (the leagues this page’s fixtures belong to), nextCursor (pass it as cursor for the following page; null once there is none) and complete (false if some league lists were temporarily unavailable — try again shortly); tz adds tz, utcFrom and utcTo

400.description:
- bad_request — date absent or malformed, sport not recognised, country sent without sport, two or more of league / category / country combined, page outside 0–99, a non-zero page alongside league, category or country, cursor combined with page, league, category or country, or a cursor that is unknown, over an hour old or issued for another sport or date

get.description:
Fixture totals for a UTC date without paging: given a sport, the date’s total and a row per category (country, region, tour) with fixture and league counts, for any date; with no sport, today’s total per sport. The liveCount field gives the number of matches currently in play.

**Note:** Dates are UTC, as on /v2/fixtures, unless you pass tz together with sport. liveCount is filled for today only (null on other dates) and comes from our live index — identical to the figure on /v2/sports — rather than from the date’s list, so a match that began yesterday may be included. Categories are sorted by fixture count, largest first; there is no live count per category because the source does not track one. With sport, fixtureCount is the sum across categories; without sport, it is the sum across sports. For one sport these totals may diverge by a few percent, since the category list includes some matches spilling over from late on the previous day. Race sports (motorsport, cycling) have no categories on this endpoint — use /v2/races. Available on all plans.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

parameters.name: date
parameters.description: UTC date as YYYY-MM-DD, defaults to today; accepts 1990-01-01 to one year ahead. If sport is omitted, only today is allowed

parameters.name: sport
parameters.description: sport slug — breaks the date’s count down by category

parameters.name: tz
parameters.description: only together with sport: counts the local day in that zone, the same window /v2/fixtures reads with that tz (an IANA zone or a fixed offset; meta repeats tz, utcFrom and utcTo). Available since 2026-11-24

get.description:
The days of /v2/fixtures in short form: one FixtureSummary row per fixture with its id, sport, league, both sides, start time, state and score. It takes the same parameters and pages the same way, by page or by cursor, the day of every sport included, but a page covers 50 leagues instead of 10: a few hundred rows, about 1,500 at most. Available since 2026-11-24.

**Note:** Built for schedules and day overviews, where a full Fixture per row would be wasted. For every sport on a date, make the first call with no cursor, then keep sending meta.nextCursor back until it comes back null; a crowded day needs a few dozen calls. For a fixture’s full detail, call /v2/fixtures/{id}.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

You get the fixtures that begin inside that local day, with start times kept in UTC, and meta reports tz plus utcFrom and utcTo, where the day begins and ends in UTC. Leave tz out and the day is a UTC one. Available since 2026-11-24

get.description:
One fixture in full: both teams, score, status, match clock, winner, league, season, round, venue, the referee (career cards per game), each team’s current manager (homeManager / awayManager — the managers who took charge of this match are on /v2/fixtures/{id}/managers) and previousLegFixtureId. That field holds our id for the first leg or the previous game in a series, and on a completed second leg aggregateWinner names the side that went through, while matchesInTie gives how many matches a knockout tie or playoff series spans (1 for a single match, 2 for two legs, 7 for best of seven). Some sports add more: seeds (homeSeed / awaySeed); in tennis, surface (hard / clay / grass / carpet, indoor), discipline (singles or doubles) and serving (who is serving at the moment); in darts, servedFirst (the side that threw the opening dart of the match); in cricket, battingSide, note, toss (winner, bat / bowl), tvUmpire and umpires; in MMA and boxing, fightResult (method, round and, for a stoppage, the time), fightCard (main card / prelims, order, weight class) and fightDiscipline (boxing, kickboxing, muayThai, …, if the source tags one); attendance (spectators, when reported); matchFormat (best of sets / legs in darts, best of games in esports); in baseball, inningState (inning, top / bottom, outs, count, runners); in basketball and (since 2026-11-23) American football, timeouts (left per side) and bonus (which sides are in the bonus); in American football, downAndDistance (down, yards to go, field position, possession, play type); in football, varCheck (a VAR review in progress and the side it concerns); finalResultOnly (true when the source has nothing beyond the result); awarded (true for a result settled off the field, by forfeit or by a ruling, rather than played out); in the UFC, homeRanking / awayRanking (the fighter’s place in the division ranking, 0 for the champion); and, in set or round sports, durations (seconds per completed set or round, plus the total).

**Note:** All score components live under periods: extra time in football and futsal is periods.extra1 / extra2, overtime in any other sport is periods.overtime, and extra innings in baseball are period10, period11, and so on. A shoot-out is never part of current — it goes in penalties — except that in ice hockey and (since 2026-11-23) floorball current includes the single goal awarded for winning a shoot-out. status.description is our own label, e.g. “Game 1”, “After overtime”, “After extra time” or “After penalties”. When the source drops coverage of a fixture, its status becomes canceled and both score sides are empty. For a match decided on penalties, winner is the shoot-out winner — second legs included, where the result on the night remains in normalTime; aggregateWinner names the side that progressed on aggregate (null if the source leaves a level aggregate unresolved). Lists and WebSocket snapshots may show aggregateWinner as null, so take it from this endpoint. Only this endpoint fills referee, homeManager / awayManager, previousLegFixtureId, toss, umpires, tvUmpire, fightCard and attendance; in fixture lists, on the live board and in WebSocket snapshots they are null (surface is filled here and on the live tennis board as well). inningState, timeouts, bonus, downAndDistance and varCheck exist only during play and are null at any other time. Every one of them except bonus is pushed in WebSocket deltas — inningState and varCheck as whole objects, timeouts and downAndDistance as partial updates (whole on first appearance, null once play stops). Because the source resends the baseball state roughly once a minute, the count may trail the action. durations — filled for tennis and the other set sports and for MMA rounds, null elsewhere — gains one period each time a set finishes, which is also delivered in WebSocket deltas (the completed period plus the updated totalSeconds; the set in progress began at clock.periodStartedAt). fightResult comes in a separate WebSocket delta, normally after the one that ends the fight, because the source publishes it only 20–60 s after the winner is known. In rugby, periods fill in live: period1 at half-time, then period2 = current − period1 through the second half; if we first fetch a fixture during the second half, both stay empty until the final whistle, and the half-time score can be taken from the period entry in /v2/fixtures/{id}/events. homeManager / awayManager reflect each club’s manager as the source lists them today: when a club has changed coach since a finished match, that match now shows the new one, and the coaches who actually led it are on /v2/fixtures/{id}/managers. Esports periods: CS records 1 for each map won and 0 otherwise; LoL records how many kills the side made in game N. serving replaces firstToServe, which carries the same value and is deprecated but still present for now. At first glance an awarded result is indistinguishable from a played one — a finished status, a winner and the awarded score, typically 3–0 — so look at awarded before treating it as played. Lists and WebSocket snapshots carry the flag as well; a fixture stored before 2026-11-18 and not fetched again since shows null. Only this endpoint reliably fills homeRanking / awayRanking (UFC fighters’ division places and, since 2026-11-23, tennis players’ ATP / WTA singles rankings); lists rarely carry them. A doubles fixture (tennis, padel, badminton, table tennis) names the two players of each pair in homeMembers / awayMembers since 2026-11-23, each with their own team id.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
Team lineups and formations plus unavailable players and the coaching staff named alongside them, with every player carrying a match rating and statistics.

**Note:** How much you get depends on the fixture: top leagues come with lineups plus per-player ratings and statistics, while many youth, amateur and friendly matches never receive any. Player statistics reuse the team-statistics keys wherever the meaning matches (passes, accuratePasses, shotsOnGoal, tackles, …; bigChancesCreated counts big chances the player set up for a teammate). Each …Percentage field is a share from 0 to 100, with one exception: basketball’s trueShootingPercentage can exceed 100 (for example a handful of free throws plus a three). Players who did not take part have rating and statistics set to null; avgRating (football) holds the player’s season average and is filled mainly before and around kick-off. The profile fields heightCm, dateOfBirth, country and marketValue mirror the player’s profile (/v2/players/{id}) and are null when the source has no value — common in predicted lineups — with marketValue largely limited to football. Preferred foot is missing because the lineups we receive lack it; the profile and the squad have it. position is a sport-dependent word (G means goalkeeper in football, goalie in ice hockey and guard in basketball), while positionCode retains the source’s letter. Ice hockey and American football use player keys of their own: goals, assists and points split into power-play, even-strength and short-handed, the goalie’s saves and shots faced broken down by strength, and on the gridiron passing, rushing, receiving, defence, fumbles, kick and punt returns, kicking and punting — the reference’s Player match statistic keys explains each one. supportStaff holds the coaches the source attaches to a side, each with our id, name, role and country (cricket names a head coach plus batting and bowling coaches); other sports return []. A fixture without lineups (so far) answers 200 with confirmed: false and both sides empty; only an unknown id gets 404. While a match is live, the data is refreshed every few seconds. Since 2026-11-23 some players carry extra statistics keys from a box score captured live: NBA games (pointsFastBreak, pointsInPaint, pointsFromTurnovers, foulsDrawn) and football matches the live tracker follows, such as MLS and Champions League games (injuries, cornerKicks, and a goalkeeper’s shotsFaced and cleanSheet).

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
Team statistics for the match, organised by period and by category.

**Note:** Coverage is graded the same way as for lineups and grows richer as the match goes on: a lower-tier fixture might offer nothing but cards, whereas a top league delivers every group. Statistic keys form one shared vocabulary across all sports (totalShots, shotsOnGoal, passes, fouls, …; the reference’s Statistic keys lists every key per sport), and group keys follow a fixed table for each sport. In American football, the team-level passingNetYards and passingYardsPerAttempt are gross figures from the source (sacks are not subtracted), whereas a player’s passingNetYards in the lineups is net. Overtime is broken down per overtime period (overtime1, overtime2, …; a single overtime is overtime1), and boxing and MMA bouts that go past the ninth round have period10, period11, … (both since 2026-11-23). NBA games (all period) and football matches the live tracker follows (injuries) carry a few extra keys from a box score captured live since 2026-11-23; the reference lists them. A fixture without statistics (yet — before kick-off, for instance) returns 200 with { "periods": [] }; you only get 404 for an id that does not exist. Data is refreshed every few seconds during a live match.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
The match’s incidents in chronological order, oldest first: goals, cards, substitutions, period markers and added-time announcements.

**Note:** Returns an empty array if the fixture has no events (yet). For an injuryTime incident, addedMinute holds the number of added minutes announced. minute is null whenever the clock is not running — before kick-off, at half-time, for bench events and during a shoot-out — and on a goal the source logs without a time (all bandy goals, some floorball goals and a basketball game’s first baskets, listed since 2026-11-23). Shoot-out kicks are listed last, in the order taken: shootoutSequence numbers them 1…N across both sides, and shootoutRound gives the kick’s position (1st, 2nd, …) within the taker’s side. A period row marks the end of a period: its period is the one just completed, so the period currently in progress has no row; in set sports its homeScore / awayScore are the sets won up to that point. period is filled on every incident. A manager booked on the bench is named in `manager`, with the minute of play in `benchMinute` (since 2026-11-26). All fields appear on every incident, set to null where irrelevant to the type, and type and detail are closed enums. Football goals carry buildUp, the chain of actions that led to the goal — shots (saved, missed, off the woodwork, penalties saved or missed), passes, crosses, free kicks, tackles, interceptions and clearances — each step with its side, player and minute, start and end pitch positions, assist, body part and expected goals, and the goal itself as the last step; buildUp is [] on all other incidents and when the source provides none. In ice hockey a penalty (type suspension) carries reason, the infraction in words, plus infraction, a stable camelCase key for it (tripping, crossChecking, …), severity (minor, major, …), the length in durationSeconds, drawnBy, and servedBy, naming whoever sat in the box in place of the offender (typically when a goalie is penalised). An NHL goal also has seasonGoals, the scorer’s season total counting this goal, and seasonAssists, the season total of every assisting player in the same order as assists. Cricket ball-by-ball and the point-level rows of set sports are not part of this list. Refreshed every few seconds during a live match.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
Text commentary from the source, one action per entry, oldest first, in football (cards, shots, corners, substitutions and more, by minute), basketball (each basket, free throw, rebound, foul and turnover) and ice hockey (face-offs, hits, blocked shots, goals, the goalkeeper leaving and returning, and penalties with who drew and who served each one). Basketball entries also give the game clock, the running score, the basket’s value and its location on the court. Ice hockey entries carry the rink zone, whether the side was at even strength, on the power play or short-handed, and the player hit or the blocker. American football entries (since 2026-11-25) add the down and distance, where the ball was spotted, who had it, run or pass, the yards the play made and the drive it belongs to.

**Note:** The English wording of each entry comes from the source as it is; DataSportsAPI does not write it. type is a closed enum, with other covering anything we have not mapped. Each entry includes every field, null where it does not apply: football uses minute / addedMinute; basketball uses periodSecond (seconds gone in the period), periodSecondsLeft (what the game clock shows), at, position / zone on the court, and scoreType on scoreChange; homeScore / awayScore appear on scoreChange (and on a football penaltyScored, carried forward from the previous goal). For an ice-hockey penalty (type suspension), player is the offender, and drawnBy, servedBy (set only when a teammate served the time), infraction and severity sit alongside. Since 2026-11-23 ice hockey has types of its own (faceOff, hit, goalkeeperOut, goalkeeperBack), scoreType goal or emptyNetGoal, zone offensive / neutral / defensive and strength on every entry; targetPlayer names who took a hit and blockedBy who stopped a shot. period gives overtime per overtime period (overtime1, overtime2, …) since 2026-11-23. If the source has no commentary, the array is empty. Since 2026-11-25 the American football fields drive, possession, down, yardsToGo, goalToGo, ballOn, playType and yardsGained are on every entry and read null in the other sports; drive is the number of a drive in /v2/fixtures/{id}/drives. Games stored before that date show null there until their play by play is read again.

**Plans:** Requires Pro, Business or Enterprise; a Free or Starter key receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
An American football game cut into its possessions, first to last. For each one: which side had the ball, the clock and period at its first and last play, what started it (kickoff, punt, turnover, …) and what finished it (touchdown, field goal, punt, turnover on downs, …), the number of plays, first downs, net and penalty yards, and how far from the end zone it started, ran its last play and got at its deepest.

**Note:** Built from the same source data as /v2/fixtures/{id}/play-by-play, where each entry's drive field holds a drive's number. Field positions are counted as yards left to the end zone the offence was attacking, so a drive from its own 35-yard line has startYardsToGoal 65. A drive still in progress has endReason null. Other sports, and games the source has no drives for, return an empty array. Live, the playByPlay frame on fixture:{id} brings the full list each time.

get.description:
Attack-momentum curve (football, plus any other sport where the source draws one) with a point for every minute: positive values mean home pressure, negative values away pressure. Tennis uses games instead — a value per game (positive when the home player took it) plus a flag for whether serve was broken.

**Note:** points is filled for football, basketball and ice hockey in covered leagues; games is filled for tennis only (where points stays empty) and is empty for all other sports. Both lists are empty before kick-off and when no graph exists. Football gives each added-time minute its own point: minute stays at the last minute of the period (45 or 90) and addedMinute runs 1, 2, …; in normal time addedMinute is null. In other sports (basketball, handball, …) a minute value ending in .5 can mark the end of a period — 45.5 is half-time. Football and ice hockey have used the curve the source draws on its own website since 2026-11-04 (see the changelog).

**Plans:** Requires Pro, Business or Enterprise; a Free or Starter key receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
All shots, oldest first, with outcome and expected goals; football gives expectedGoals / expectedGoalsOnTarget, pitch and goal-mouth coordinates, body part and situation, ice hockey technique and strength. Ice hockey shots also carry rink coordinates; basketball serves one team per request, listing each of its field-goal attempts as made, missed or blocked along with its court location.

**Note:** Available for football, ice hockey and basketball in covered leagues; any other case returns an empty array. In football and ice hockey, outcome is goal | save | miss | block | post, and a football shot cleared off the line counts as a block. In basketball the outcomes are goal (made), miss and block; positions are measured from the basket in tenths of a foot, and each team’s chart takes a request of its own (team=home, team=away). Since 2026-11-22 player= returns one player’s shots instead, each with the quarter it came in (period); in the team charts the player and time fields stay null. Only ice hockey uses technique (wrist, snap, slap, …) and strength. goalType is regular, ownGoal or penalty. Shoot-out kicks appear at the end: shootoutSequence is the order of kicks across both teams (matching the events), and shootoutRound is the kick’s number (1st, 2nd, …) for the taker’s side. In football, period (since 2026-10-24; null for earlier data) is derived from the minute: period1, period2, extra1, extra2, or penalties for a shoot-out kick. While a match is live the list is re-read every few seconds; fixture:{id} WebSocket channels (Business and Enterprise) receive the entire list as a shotmap frame whenever it changes.

**Plans:** Requires Pro, Business or Enterprise; a Free or Starter key receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
A point-by-point breakdown of the match. Tennis nests sets → games (server, winner, set score) → points; badminton, table tennis and volleyball nest sets → rallies, with the running score. Cricket nests innings → overs → balls: each ball has its batter, bowler, outcome, runs, extras, wicket and dismissal, and the score after the delivery, and since 2026-11-04 also the source’s commentary text for each ball, the wagon wheel (zone, angle and distance of the shot) and the pitching spot. Baseball lists at-bats with inning, top / bottom, batting side, batter and pitcher, plus the home side’s win probability before and after the at-bat. Darts nests sets → legs (starting score, first thrower, winner, checkout) → visits (visit score, both sides’ remaining totals, checkout).

**Note:** format names the one list that holds data (tennis and rally sports: sets; cricket: innings; baseball: atBats; darts: darts); every other list is empty. Darts visits do not break down into individual darts, as the source has none; a match played in legs is represented as a single set. On cricket balls (since 2026-11-04), commentary carries the source’s English text (null below the top tiers). shot describes the wagon wheel: zone is the fielding sector, as seen for a right-handed batter ( squareLeg, fineLeg, behindWicket, thirdMan, point, coverPoint, cover, longOff, straight, longOn, midWicket), angle in degrees (0 square leg, 90 behind the keeper, 180 point, 270 straight) and distance on a 1–5 scale (5 = reached the boundary); it is null when the batter did not hit the ball. pitchedAt gives where the ball pitched, in the source’s own units, with y growing with distance from the batter (about 25 for a yorker, 41 for a good length, 54 for a short ball). Each baseball at-bat states how likely a home win was at that point (0–100, a figure the source calculates) and, since 2026-11-04, carries an id for /v2/fixtures/{id}/at-bats/{atBatId}/pitches, where the last pitch listed ends the at-bat with its result. Any other sport, or a match with no point-by-point data yet, gets 200 with format null and every list empty. For rally sports you only get the rallies the source captured; lower tiers may skip some, which shows up as a jump in the running score. Each tennis point holds the score after it (homeScore / awayScore such as "15" or "A"; null on the game-winning point added at the end), a description (ace or doubleFault) and homeType / awayType (one of won, breakPoint, setPoint, miniBreak, none). In a match tie-break, the deciding set holds it as its only game, played to 10. Refreshed every few seconds during a live match.

**Plans:** Requires Pro, Business or Enterprise; a Free or Starter key receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
Full cricket scorecard by innings: total, extras, batting card (runs, balls, fours, sixes, strike rate, state, dismissal, bowler, fielder) and bowling card (overs, maidens, runs, wickets, economy, wides, no-balls). Falls of wicket and partnerships follow.

**Note:** Any other sport, or a cricket match before the first delivery, returns 200 with an empty innings list. Overs follow cricket notation, so 19.3 is 19 overs plus 3 balls; once an over is complete the figure moves up to the next whole number (5 rather than the source’s 4.6), and the same goes for falls of wicket. Partnerships are frequently missing for multi-day matches. Refreshed every few seconds during a live match. For ball by ball — who faced and who bowled each delivery — use /v2/fixtures/{id}/events (or /points).

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
Baseball only: one at-bat pitch by pitch — type (MLB Statcast categories: four-seam fastball, sinker, cutter, changeup, curveball, slider, sweeper, …), zone, release speed, result, count and outs after each. Each pitch also carries the score, the batted ball (trajectory, hardness) and what the runners and fielders did. Plays that happen between pitches, such as a stolen-base attempt, appear as rows with kind steal.

**Note:** Other sports get 200 and an empty array. balls / strikes / outs reflect the count AFTER the pitch, and the final pitch (endsAtBat true) carries the at-bat’s result as its outcome. outcome comes from a closed set; when it is other, outcomeCode holds the source’s own code. zone follows MLB Statcast numbering (1–9 inside the strike zone, 11–14 outside it). speedKmh holds the release speed in km/h; multiply it by 0.6214 for mph. For runners, fromBase 0 is the batter, toBase 4 means a run scored, and toBase is null when the runner was put out. Lists saved before 2026-11-04 show AtBat.id as null until they are refreshed.

**Plans:** Requires Pro, Business or Enterprise; a Free or Starter key receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
Returns one page of a team’s fixtures, either recent or upcoming.

**Note:** If the team exists but has nothing to list, the response is 200 with an empty array. Since 2026-10-24 every competitor list splits matches the same way. upcoming holds matches not yet started (including ones postponed to a future date), soonest first, and page 0 also includes a next match that the source has filed under recent (tennis players, fighters). recent holds live, finished and called-off matches, with the newest at the top of every page. For a live or just-finished match, status, score and clock are accurate to the second. Once a match kicks off it moves to recent on your next request, and both lists are rebuilt on the first request after any of the team’s matches ends, is rescheduled or is postponed (see Update times). A padel player’s list holds his matches, each of them played as half of a pair (since 2026-11-23).

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
Shows how a team lines up as the source records it. Ice hockey: the forward lines (left wing, centre and right wing of lines 1–4), the defence pairs (left and right of pairs 1–4), the goaltenders in order (1 is the starter, 2 the backup) and both power-play units (five places each). Baseball (since 2026-11-23): the starting pitchers in rotation order, the relievers, the closer, and who covers each place in the field from catcher to designated hitter, first choice first. Available since 2026-11-23.

**Note:** Ice hockey (NHL) and baseball teams have one so far; any other team returns an empty array. A player is listed once for every slot he holds, so a first-line centre often turns up again on a power-play unit. The chart is read together with the squad, so it is as current as /squad (a day at most).

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

**Note:** Keys use the same vocabulary as match statistics (totalShots, shotsOnGoal, cornerKicks, passes, averageRating, …), paired with an …Against variant that holds what opponents recorded — in football bigChancesAgainst, shotsOnGoalAgainst, cornerKicksAgainst and so on, in basketball pointsAgainst, fieldGoalPercentageAgainst, reboundsAgainst and so on. Basketball adds advanced metrics as well: offensiveRating, defensiveRating, netRating, pace, trueShootingPercentage, effectiveFieldGoalPercentage and assistTurnoverRatio. The reference’s Season statistic keys defines every football, basketball and rugby key. A matches value of 0 is dropped when the other counts are non-zero.

get.description:
A player’s past twelve months as one timeline, oldest first: every match he played with his rating, minutes, goals, assists and expected goals, the matches he sat on the bench or missed (with the reason), his injuries and his transfers, plus the leagues those lines refer to.

**Note:** Each line has a type (match, bench, missing, injury, transfer). The match figures are filled on match lines only and are null on the others; missingReason is set on missing lines. Football and ice hockey only, for the players the source tracks this way; anyone else gets two empty lists. Lines dated before your plan’s history are left out, and meta.historyFrom then gives the first day included.

**Plans:** Requires Pro, Business or Enterprise; a Free or Starter key receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
Key figures for a season — running totals such as goals, home and away wins, draws and cards — plus the teams new to the division, whether relegated into it from above or promoted from below.

**Note:** The statistic keys come from our data source and differ between sports. hostCountries lists a tournament’s host nations as Country objects — CA, MX and US for the 2026 World Cup; eleven hosts for EURO 2020, with England as EN and Scotland as SX — and stays empty for a regular league season. prizeMoney is the season’s total purse together with its currency, and tier is how the source grades an esports tournament — a lowercase letter, with "s" at the top followed by "a", "b", "c" and so on; either one is null when the source gives no value. A season with no figures still answers 200, with empty statistics and lists; only an unknown id, or a season from another league, gets 404.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
League tables for a single season. With no extra parameters you get the one table marked primary for the season — the league table, or in a group stage the first group; meta.overall tells you whether it includes every team. Add group=all to get every table (conferences, divisions, groups), or type=home / type=away for a table built from home or away games alone.

**Note:** A season may hold several tables, listed in our data source’s order — for example two conferences, four divisions and a league table in the NHL, two conferences and an overall table in MLS, and one table per group at a World Cup. Exactly one table is flagged primary and served by default — the league table if there is one, otherwise the largest table, and the first group when all are the same size. overall is true solely for a table that contains every team in the season. position always runs 1..n; we re-rank rows whenever the source’s numbering does not. A column that does not apply to a sport is null — the NBA ranks on winPercentage, so its points column is null; draws is null in any table where a draw is impossible (basketball, ice hockey, baseball, volleyball, …); overtimeLosses is filled in ice hockey, as are regulationWins / regulationLosses on tables that carry them (KHL, SHL, AHL and the NHL’s league table, whose conference and division tables show only the regulation losses), and shootoutWins / shootoutLosses where shoot-outs are tallied separately — in the KHL, where overtimeWins then counts overtime alone and the overtime-only defeats work out as overtimeLosses minus shootoutLosses; scoresFor / scoresAgainst are measured in scoreUnit (goals, points, runs, sets, …); streak (+3 means three straight wins, −2 two straight losses) appears where the source provides it (NBA, EuroLeague, Liga ACB, …). form, added on 2026-10-24, lists up to five of the team’s most recent results in this competition season, oldest first — only home or only away results in the home / away tables — and is null where the source has none. Football publishes split home / away tables, and so do a number of basketball, handball, volleyball and ice-hockey competitions — the KHL, the SuperLega, Liga ACB, the EuroLeague and the Handball-Bundesliga among them. The NBA and NHL publish none and the NFL stops updating its versions, so for those three sports (basketball, ice hockey, American football) we compute them ourselves (meta.source computed) from the finished regular-season fixtures: a home row counts only home games, an away row only away games. They carry only the columns that the same method, run over every game, reproduces exactly for the overall table (NBA: wins, losses, winPercentage, gamesBehind within each table, scores; NFL: wins, losses, draws, winPercentage, scores; NHL: wins, losses, overtimeLosses — defeats in overtime or a shoot-out — and points at 2 per win plus 1 per overtime loss, scores). In those sports a published home / away table that lacks games is swapped for the computed one. In winPercentage a tie is worth half a win. Rows are ordered by points or win share, with ties broken by wins and then score difference — head-to-head is never used. Updated once a day. losses always counts every defeat, so wins + draws + losses = played; for the NHL seasons 2013/14 to 2020/21, where the source counted regulation losses only, the overtime losses were added on 2026-11-23 and the regulation figure moved to regulationLosses. Leagues that settle relegation on an average over several seasons (the source's “Promedios” tables) get that table as one more group with group=all, never as the default: its rows rank by pointsPerGame and show the seasons behind it in pointsThisSeason, pointsPreviousSeason and pointsTwoSeasonsAgo (since 2026-11-27; null in every other table).

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
A season’s fixtures: either one round exactly as our data source lists it (round), or one page of the season’s recent or upcoming matches (type + page).

**Note:** In a knockout round only matches with both sides known appear: the source leaves out a match whose side is still a placeholder (the winner of a tie not yet played), so a round in which no side is settled comes back empty. /v2/leagues/{id}/cup-trees lists all slots, settled or still open, together with their fixture ids. type (since 2026-11-19) pages through the whole season regardless of rounds: upcoming covers matches not yet started (or postponed to a later date), soonest first; recent covers matches already under way, completed or called off, with the latest first. /v2/teams/{id}/fixtures divides matches by the same rule. A page beyond the last returns an empty list. Since 2026-11-25, page 0 of upcoming also carries matches whose start time has passed without them beginning, as a team's list does; a match the source keeps in its own recent list stays in recent even if it never began (a padel walkover). A round asked for without its slug, when /rounds lists one, is served from that single slug; if /rounds lists several, the answer is 400 and the message names them. For a match in play, status, score and clock are accurate to the second.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
Season leaderboards per statistic (rating, goals, assists, xG, tackles, saves and more; up to 50 players each at our data source), paged with limit players per board (10 by default), or one board via category.

**Note:** Paging slices every leaderboard at the same places, so page 1 with limit 10 returns places 11–20 of each one. For a statistic’s complete top 50, request category=goals&limit=50 (a single leaderboard, about 20 KB) rather than every leaderboard at that depth (32 in football, roughly 550 KB at 50 entries each). The available categories depend on the sport (around 30 in football; points, rebounds, assists, … in basketball) and reuse the statistic key names (averageRating, goals, cleanSheets, goalInvolvements, …). statistic tells you which key inside each entry’s statistics the leaderboard is ranked on — football’s mostConceded / leastConceded, for instance, rank on goalsConceded. If type is omitted, the season’s default applies (regularSeason for the NBA, NHL, …). Leagues, seasons or types that have no leaderboards yield an empty array.

Returns every race that has a session beginning on a given UTC day. Each race’s sessions are served by /v2/races/{id}/sessions.

**Note:** A day lists no more than 40 races. A race weekend shows up on each day on which one of its sessions begins. You get the fixtures that begin inside that local day, with start times kept in UTC, and meta reports tz plus utcFrom and utcTo, where the day begins and ends in UTC. Leave tz out and the day is a UTC one. Available since 2026-11-24

get.description:
One race in full: series, season, round, status, dates, winner, circuit (motorsport: name, city, country, lap length, map image), host country, laps and distance, and category (cycling). Its sessions are served by /v2/races/{id}/sessions.

**Note:** startDate is the UTC day the first session or stage runs once we hold the sessions (motorsport too since 2026-11-25), otherwise the day our data source gives the event; endDate is the source's. Sessions have exact timestamps. winner refers to the main race — for a cycling stage race, the general classification — and is filled once it has finished. circuit.lengthMeters is given for Formula 1 and NASCAR (converted from miles) and distanceMeters for Formula 1; where only the race session holds laps and distance (NASCAR), both are null here — read them from /sessions. MotoGP has laps only. circuit.image is a circuit map hosted on our CDN, drawn in light lines over a dark background, or null when the source has none.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
Every session of a race, earliest first — practice, sprint, qualifying (split into parts Q1, Q2…) and the race itself, or the stages of a cycling race. Each comes with its type, status and start time, laps and distance, weather, track condition, temperatures and safety car, the winner and, in cycling, the stage towns and profile.

**Note:** Pass a session id, or a part id from parts, as session= to /results and /laps. get.description:
A race’s classification. In motorsport that is the main race session (the last of type race), named in meta.session, with grid, pit stops, tyre stints, the set now fitted (currentTyre: compound, new or used), inPit (true while the car sits in the pit lane during a running session), best laps and points; for a cycling stage race it is the general classification, with every rider’s secondary classifications (points, mountains, young rider, jersey). Pass session= to get one session instead (a practice, a qualifying, a stage) or one qualifying part (Q1, Q2… — part ids are listed by /v2/races/{id}/sessions). When the source stores a knock-out qualifying only part by part (MotoGP), the session’s table is now built from those parts (since 2026-11-28; it used to come back empty): everyone in the final part in their order (Q2: places 1–12), followed by those eliminated in each earlier part, in that part’s order. Every part can still be read by itself through its id.

**Note:** state is one of classified, didNotFinish, didNotStart, disqualified or notClassified, read from each row's own status (since 2026-11-25). Anyone outside the classification has position null, and our data source may also skip a place. timeMs holds the total time for a race or stage, or the best lap for practice and qualifying. Those who are out, rows with no time of their own beyond a +0.000 filler from the source, and classified riders whose time the source did not record (cycling) get null in all three of timeMs, gapMs and intervalMs. Since 2026-11-28 a classified row keeps any time, gap or interval the source does give it, even when it is laps down (see lapsBehind). tyreStints is filled for Formula 1 races only; cycling is null except on the overall result of a stage race. part is deprecated and always null, as nothing has been merged from parts since 2026-11-19. To read a part, pass its id as session=; there timeMs is the best lap and carNumber is null, because the source does not number a part’s rows: look each competitor up in the session’s own table instead. As long as a session is running (a practice, or a knock-out qualifying), the source holds nothing for the session itself but the entry list, with no places or times until the flag falls; since 2026-11-27 we answer with the live order of the part now running instead (Q1, Q2, Q3, or a practice’s single part: places, laps, times and gaps), and the race:{id} snapshot carries the same table. Since 2026-11-25 a one-day cycling race answers with the race session itself by default, which brings start numbers and each rider's gap to the one ahead. A called-off session that still has a ranked classification returns it rather than an empty list. After a session ends, inPit reads null throughout its table and the tables of its parts.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
A single search over teams (individual competitors included), players, managers, referees, leagues, fixtures, racing series and races; each hit’s type names the endpoint family its id is valid for — /v2/teams, /v2/players, /v2/managers, /v2/referees, /v2/leagues, /v2/fixtures, /v2/series and /v2/races. Venues have a search of their own: pass type=venue for ids that work with /v2/venues/{id}. So do football player agencies: type=agency (since 2026-11-23) returns ids for /v2/agencies/{id}. Player hits include the player’s current team; fixture hits include the teams, league, start time and status; venue hits include city, country and capacity.

**Note:** This API models every competitor as a team, so tennis players and other individual-sport athletes are returned with type team. type is a closed set — manager, referee, series and race were added on 2026-10-24, fixture and venue on 2026-11-04 — so ignore any value your client does not recognise. Three fields depend on the type and are null for all others: venue (a Venue), team (the player’s current team, as a TeamRef) and fixture ({ home, away, league, startTime, status }, with status as the coarse StatusType — the score and the rest come from /v2/fixtures/{id}). Venue hit ids work with /v2/venues/{id} and match the id in Fixture.venue and TeamDetail.venue. Since 2026-11-04 team hits include gender (male | female | mixed, matching TeamDetail), which lets you mark a women’s team without a call to /v2/teams/{id}; it is null for every other type. Venue hits come from a separate search at the source and are returned only with type=venue; the mixed list has none. The same goes for agency hits and type=agency. Passing type (since 2026-11-09) restricts the list to that type, returns 20 hits per page and reaches much further than the mixed list: ask for ?q=smith&type=player and pages go up to 50; hasNextPage stays true as long as a page is full. type=series is read from the mixed list, as the source has no search of its own for series. The mixed list pages as well since 2026-11-23, 20 hits a page with hasNextPage, and an empty page always says hasNextPage false. type=player also returns athletes of individual sports (Novak Djokovic, Max Verstappen) as hits of type team, whose ids belong to /v2/teams; type=team lists the teams first and then the individual competitors of the page, so a type=team page can hold more than 20 hits. Since 2026-11-23 hits also carry country (teams, players, managers, referees, agencies), national (teams), and position, positionCode and retired (players; deceased since 2026-11-24), and since 2026-11-24 a manager hit names his team. Managers and referees also get image, a photo on our CDN (since 2026-11-04; null if the source has none); series, races, fixtures and venues always have image null. Paging and league hits changed on 2026-11-25: hasNextPage is true whenever any list behind the page still has more, so a type=team page reports more when only individual competitors remain, and a type=series page reports none when no further series exist. League and series hits carry category, the country, region (International, for instance), tour or game they are filed under, and league hits fill country and gender. A side the source names as mixed (a badminton team event, say) has gender mixed.

**Plans:** Every plan, Free included.

get.description:
All markets the bookmaker offers on a fixture — result (1X2), double chance, draw no bet, winner, first to score, both teams to score, Asian handicap, handicap / point spread, goal / card / corner / points totals, the cricket toss winner, most sixes, a hundred / fifty in the match, and next goal (live). Each comes with opening and current prices in decimal and fractional form, the direction of the latest price change, its suspension state and, once the match is over, the winning selections. Available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans.

**Note:** An empty markets list with updatedAt null is a normal answer: the bookmaker has no prices for that fixture, which is common in minor leagues and for matches far in the future. Telling markets apart: key is fixed for the life of the fixture and is made of the kind plus, where they apply, :period, :line and :live ("result", "result:half1", "totalGoals:2.5", "asianHandicap:-1.25", "winner:live"). Match the markets of a WebSocket odds frame to the ones you hold by this key. line is the figure of a total or the handicap given to the HOME side, and a line that moves makes a market with a new key. Once the match is in play, two markets of a kind stand side by side: the in-play one (live: true, key ending …:live) and the pre-match one, now closed and frozen at its last prices before kick-off. Prices: decimal is 1 + fractional, rounded to 2 decimal places. Settlement: winning stays null until somebody settles the market, and settledBy names who did. "source" is the usual case, and the quick one: within minutes of the end it has flagged goal totals, winners and results. "computed" marks two football markets we have settled ourselves from the final result since 2026-11-12, never overriding a flag the source has set: an Asian handicap on a half line, judged on the regular-time score, and total cards on a half line, provided the match saw yellow cards only, all shown to players on the pitch, and its incidents and statistics agree. No other unsettled market will ever get a flag: its winning stays null. Our checks found such gaps on NBA games, where the point spread (handicap) and the first-quarter winner were still null hours after full time (2026-11-05), and in football, where days after the final whistle no finished fixture had its Asian handicaps or its total cards settled (2026-11-12). Whatever the flag says, a bet is decided by the bookmaker’s own rules. Freshness: REST copies are renewed every few seconds in play, and the odds:{id} channel delivers every price change.

**Plans:** Requires Pro, Business or Enterprise; a Free or Starter key receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
Two percentages for each side of a fixture, expectedWinPercentage and actualWinPercentage, which show whether the market rates that side too high or too low. The first is the chance the side’s win price implies; the second is how often sides at that price have gone on to win. Both are figures of our data source, not our own. Available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans.

**Note:** Reading the answer: there are at most two entries, home and away, and never one for a draw. An entry is null if the source lacks figures for that side, which can happen to one side alone; when it does not cover the fixture at all (most minor leagues, doubles, matches far in the future), both entries and updatedAt are null. Do not expect the price in an entry to be one of the opening or current prices that /v2/fixtures/{id}/odds returns: for these figures the source picks a pre-match price of its own. The two percentages: expectedWinPercentage is roughly 100 / decimal, rounded, with the bookmaker’s margin still in it. actualWinPercentage rests on the source’s record of sides at that price, and the source publishes neither the size of that sample nor the period it spans. Refresh: the same as the odds, about every 30 seconds during play.

**Plans:** Requires Pro, Business or Enterprise; a Free or Starter key receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
The betting markets a bookmaker prices next to a fixture's team streaks — match goals, both teams to score, cards, corners, first to score and the result. One list (general) sits beside the sides' recent-form streaks, the other (headToHead) beside their head-to-head streaks. Pair them with /v2/fixtures/{id}/streaks, for instance by placing the 2.5 match-goals prices next to a team's “More than 2.5 goals 7/7”. Available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans.

**Note:** The streaks themselves are on /v2/fixtures/{id}/streaks, on every plan; this endpoint only adds the prices. Markets share the /v2/fixtures/{id}/odds shape: key, kind, line, opening and current prices, the live and suspended flags, and winning once settled. Each list keeps the bookmaker's ordering, holds no market twice, and starts with the market the bookmaker features — the natural pick if you display just one. No market is linked to a particular streak, so match them up by kind when needed: goal streaks go with totalGoals, “Both teams scoring” with bothTeamsToScore, card and corner streaks with totalCards and totalCorners, “First to score” / “First to concede” with firstToScore, and the win, loss and draw streaks with result. When the bookmaker prices nothing, both lists are empty and updatedAt is null; in practice football in the larger leagues has them, while the basketball and ice-hockey fixtures we sampled had none. Refresh timing matches the odds endpoints. 18+ only; please gamble responsibly.

**Plans:** Requires Pro, Business or Enterprise; a Free or Starter key receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
Which tracking data a fixture holds (Enterprise only): its sport and coordinate frame, startedAt (taken from the fixture’s own start), a final flag once the match is over, a complete flag once the post-match read is in, how many ball frames, how many tracked events and how many timeline entries it holds.

**Note:** Two flags tell you when to read again: final turns true when the match is over, and complete when the post-match read is in, which happens between a few minutes and an hour after the end (a trackingStatus frame announces it on the WebSocket). Fetch the events and the timeline again once complete is true, because the passes of a football match, most of its event details and the basketball events exist only from then on. Before that you have what arrives live: in football the goals, shots, cards, substitutions, set pieces and flow of play, each about 9 seconds after it happened (roughly 15 at most), and in basketball, ice hockey and darts the timeline, about 5 seconds behind (table tennis and American football, since 2026-11-24, about a second) (on the WebSocket, the timelineEvent frames). The ball track is a different case: it is made of the frames the source captured live, and a frame missed during play is never filled in later.

**Plans:** Requires the Enterprise plan; every other plan receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
Every tracked event with its position, in the order of play, on Enterprise only — football passes from start to end point, set pieces, shots, cards, fouls, substitutions and the attacking flow; tennis serves, faults and points (each with the game score after it), plus where the ball and the players were; basketball shots and where they were taken, rebounds, fouls and turnovers. Up to 1,000 per page, optionally narrowed to one type or to events after an instant.

**Note:** What the list holds depends on the sport and on the moment. Ice hockey, darts, table tennis, American football and baseball have no tracked events at all: their play lives in /tracking/timeline and in the timelineEvent frames on the WebSocket, and most basketball matches return none until the post-match read. A football match fills the list while it is played, at around 18 events a minute: flowAttack / flowDangerousAttack / flowBallSafe, where side is the team in possession and position is where the ball is, so that together they give the current state of play; possessionChange, which has no side; and goal, attemptAtGoal, corner, freeKick, throwIn, goalKick, yellowCard, redCard, substitution, possibleGoal / possibleCorner and more. Passes join them with the post-match read. Reading an event: key never changes, and the trackedEvent frame of the same event carries the identical key, so a pushed copy and a REST copy can be matched. The clock fields follow the sport: minute and second in football, set and game in tennis, period in basketball. A null player, assist, playerIn or playerOut means the source gave no name, or gave one the squad list does not contain. Entries that only keep the clock are never listed.

**Plans:** Requires the Enterprise plan; every other plan receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
The timeline of a basketball, ice hockey, darts, football, tennis, table tennis, American football or baseball match, oldest first (Enterprise only; football and tennis joined on 2026-11-23, table tennis and American football on 2026-11-24, and these four run a second or two behind play). Since 2026-11-13 it fills while the match is played, each entry roughly 5 seconds after the moment itself: every shot and where it was taken (made or missed; on target, blocked or saved), goals with the scorer and assists, penalties and their length, faceoffs, hits, timeouts and the score of each period — and in darts each dart with the bed it landed in and each visit with its score, the points left to get, and the legs and sets.

**Note:** Basketball, ice hockey and darts have a timeline, and since 2026-11-23 football (corners, free kicks and other restarts, attempts on goal, goals, cards, changes, VAR checks and period changes, each located on the pitch grid) and tennis (serves, faults, every change of score and each set); since 2026-11-24 table tennis (every point with the game score it left, who serves next and whether it set up or won a game or the match) and American football (every play with the ball’s spot in yards, down and distance, the result, the yards gained and the players by name; a play is revised in place as details come in); since 2026-11-27 baseball, one entry per pitch and per play, with the count, the outs and the runners on base after it in `baseball`, and no positions at all. Football, tennis, table tennis and American football are recorded live only, so a match not captured live returns an empty list. Treat a live timeline as provisional: the source can correct an event or take it back while the match is in play, and events it withdrew are left out, as is clock housekeeping; since 2026-11-28 a football goal cancelled after a VAR review is dropped too, though the source keeps it on record. Read the list again, or follow tracking:{id}, to stay in step. On the 0–100 grid of basketball and ice hockey, x = 100 is the end home plays towards and x = 0 the end away plays towards, for the whole match. That orientation is ours, because the source does not say which way a team attacks: its ice hockey spots swap ends every period, and some basketball games swap baskets at half-time. So for each side and period we look at where its shots fall and, when they fall in the wrong half, mirror that side’s positions for the period (x → 100 − x, y → 100 − y). When a side has no shots in a period, its direction is taken from the opponent and from the neighbouring periods, which is why, in a live match, an event from a period that has no shots yet can still move once shots arrive (it is sent as an upsert frame). Since 2026-11-27 basketball timeline y is flipped to 100 − y before it is served, as football's has been since 2026-11-23: the source measures it from the sideline opposite to its tracked events, and after the flip a shot has one x and one y in this list, in timelineEvent frames and in /tracking/events alike. A client that flipped basketball timeline y itself should stop doing so. For basketball, look for type goal with points set: that is a made basket. Darts events carry no position, and some darts competitions are reported visit by visit only. The darts types, from the result down: matchWon and setWon close the match and the set; legWon has the legs in homeScore / awayScore; checkout is the visit that took the leg, with checkoutDouble; a visit carries darts.score as the visit total, dartsThrown, remaining (what each side still needs), legs and sets; and a dartThrow carries darts.score, number, multiplier, ring (single, double, treble, outerBull, bull or miss), doubleAttempt and bed, which since 2026-11-13 gives, for a single, the inner or outer single bed as the source reports it and is null for every other ring.

**Plans:** Requires the Enterprise plan; every other plan receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

post.description:
Queues the export of one league season and answers 202 at once with the new export in status pending; the files come later, through the status call. The JSON body says what to build: league (a DataSportsAPI league id), season (an id that /v2/leagues/{id}/seasons lists for that league) and, optionally, format. With json, the default, you get one file, season.json, which holds every fixture of the season with its rounds, the standings, the top players and the top teams, and the league and season objects themselves, all exactly as their endpoints return them. The fixtures and the standings come as two flat tables instead when you ask for csv or parquet.

**Note:** Columns of the two tables in a csv or parquet export — fixtures: fixture_id, sport, start_time, round, round_name, status, status_description, home_team_id, home_team, away_team_id, away_team, home_score, away_score, winner, venue; standings: table, primary, position, team_id, team, played, wins, draws, losses, scores_for, scores_against, points, zone. Two things to check in a finished export. It can be ready and still incomplete: its error field then names what could not be read (“not included: topPlayers”), and because fixtures are gathered through the rounds of the season, a competition our data source does not split into rounds (NBA and NHL regular seasons) comes out with no fixtures at all. And it can list a match twice: we mirror the source’s own listing, in which a match that was postponed and played later stands once as the postponed fixture and once as the played one, each under its own id (Premier League 25/26: 381 fixtures, one of them postponed).

**Plans:** Requires Business or Enterprise; any lower plan receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

get.description:
One export: where its build stands and, once status is ready, a download link for every file. The links in files are valid for one hour, until linksExpireAt, and each further call issues new ones. While the build runs, call again every few seconds and stop when status is ready or failed. A season that is already cached is done within seconds; any other takes up to a few minutes.

**Plans:** Requires Business or Enterprise; any lower plan receives 403 endpoint_not_in_plan.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: export id issued by DataSportsAPI, a positive integer

400.description: Bad request (`bad_request`): the message lists the values the parameter accepts.

401.description: Missing, unknown or revoked API key (`unauthorized`). Not counted against the quota.

403.description: Refused, and not counted against the quota: your plan does not include this endpoint (`endpoint_not_in_plan`), the requested data lies before your plan's history window (`history_not_in_plan`; see `error.historyFrom`), or the caller's address is not the one on the account's IP allowlist (`ip_not_allowed`; the allowlist is part of every plan and holds one address or CIDR range).

404.description: Not found (`not_found`), valid ids with no source data behind them (`no_data`, e.g. tracking of a fixture the source does not follow), or the player-statistics explorer asked for a league that is not football (`not_supported`).

429.description: Per-minute rate exceeded (`rate_limited`, not counted against the quota) or the period's quota spent (`quota_exceeded`); wait the `Retry-After` seconds. `error.upgradeUrl` is the pricing page.

post.description:
Issues a one-time ticket for opening a connection, valid for 30 seconds. The call is authenticated, rate-limited and counted against your usage exactly like any other /v2 request, and it takes no request body.

**Plans:** Requires Business or Enterprise; on a lower plan the ticket request returns 403 ws_not_available. The tracking:{id} channel needs Enterprise and is refused on Business with channel_forbidden.
